text: Every table inside the Log Analytics workspace needs something to write into it, and that something is a data connector. No connector means no data, no matter how good your detection logic ends up being later. Sentinel ships with dozens of built-in connectors, and choosing the right ones is one of the first real decisions a Sentinel deployment makes.

Connectors fall into three main types. Service-to-service connectors are cloud-native, Azure pulling data directly from another Microsoft service's API with nothing to install — turning one on is close to a single toggle. Agent-based connectors use a small piece of software installed on a machine that isn't cloud-native. API-based connectors pull from sources like another cloud provider entirely, through an API rather than an agent.

Real service-to-service examples: the Microsoft Entra ID connector brings in sign-in logs and audit logs, the Office 365 connector brings in SharePoint, Exchange, and Teams activity, and connectors for Defender products like Defender for Endpoint forward their own detections straight into Sentinel. Because these already speak the same cloud-to-cloud language, they're typically the fastest to stand up and the most reliable to keep running.

For machines that aren't cloud-native, Sentinel uses the Azure Monitor Agent, installed directly on a Windows server, a Linux machine, or on-prem hardware, to forward logs up to the workspace. That's how Sentinel collects raw Windows Security Events from a domain controller, or Syslog and CEF data from Linux servers and third-party firewalls that need to show up in the same SOC.

AWS CloudTrail is the clearest API-based example: Sentinel's AWS connector authenticates into an AWS account using a cross-account role and an S3 bucket where CloudTrail deposits its logs, then pulls that activity in through an API-based path rather than an installed agent. Sources with no pre-built connector at all can still come in through a codeless or custom API integration.

Once configured, the Data Connectors page shows a status — most commonly Connected — and which table the data is landing in, tying straight back to the table names from the last lesson. A connector not showing Connected is always the first thing to check before assuming a rule's logic is broken. Next: what all this ingested data actually costs.
